sun.polarDay: The sun does not set on this date: {city} is inside the polar day.
sun.polarNight: The sun does not rise on this date: {city} is inside the polar night.
city.dstCount: Clocks in {city} change {count} times in {year}. The next changes:
hub.abbreviationsNote: Sixteen abbreviations, every direction between them. Each page names the IANA zone it computes with, and flags the letters that mean more than one thing.
dst.neverChangeNote: {count} of the {total} cities covered here keep the same offset all year, either because their country never adopted daylight saving or because it abandoned it.
dst.tableNote: {count} changes across {cities} cities. Rows already in the past are dimmed.
epoch.knownNote: Fixed points in the count. These do not change, so they are part of the page rather than something your browser has to compute.
overlap.commonShapesNote: Computed for a 09:00–18:00 day at the last rebuild. These are structural — they change only when a country changes its rules.
diff.neverChanges: Neither place changes its clocks, so this difference is the same all year.
diff.workedExample: A worked example: New York and London
diff.workedExampleNote: The most-searched pair on the internet, and a good illustration of why “five hours” is a half-truth. These dates come from the IANA database at build time — they are fixed facts, not a live reading.
utc.fromElsewhere: What UTC looks like from elsewhere
utc.fromElsewhereNote: Each city’s offset from UTC, as it stands at the time of the last rebuild. Cities that observe daylight saving move by an hour twice a year — their city page has the exact dates.
pair.summary.same.1: {from} and {to} are on the same clock: both keep {zone} time, so there is never a difference between them.
pair.summary.same.2: There is no time difference between {from} and {to} — both cities sit in the same time zone, and their clocks change together.
pair.summary.ahead.1: {to} is {gap} ahead of {from} right now, so midday in {from} lands in the {landing} in {to}.
pair.summary.ahead.2: Right now {to} runs {gap} ahead of {from}. That gap is not fixed: it moves when either city changes its clocks.
pair.summary.behind.1: {to} is {gap} behind {from} right now, so midday in {from} lands in the {landing} in {to}.
pair.summary.behind.2: Right now {to} runs {gap} behind {from}. That gap is not fixed: it moves when either city changes its clocks.
pair.tableIntro.1: Every hour of a day in {from}, and what the clock reads in {to} at that same moment.
pair.tableIntro.2: The whole day mapped across: read down the left for {from}, across for {to}.
pair.dst.neither.1: Neither {from} nor {to} changes its clocks, so the difference between them is the same every day of the year.
pair.dst.neither.2: Both cities keep one offset all year. Whatever difference holds today still holds in six months.
pair.dst.both.1: Both cities change their clocks, but not necessarily on the same date — which is why the difference between them shifts for a few weeks each year.
pair.dst.both.2: {from} and {to} both observe daylight saving. Where their change dates differ, so does the gap between them for the weeks in between.
pair.dst.one.1: {changing} changes its clocks; {stable} does not. The difference between them therefore shifts by an hour twice a year.
pair.dst.one.2: {stable} keeps one offset all year while {changing} moves twice. That is the whole reason this difference is seasonal.
pair.call.none.1: There is no hour where both cities are inside a 09:00–18:00 working day. Someone has to move — the nearest workable windows are below.
pair.call.none.2: A standard working day in {from} and one in {to} do not overlap at all. Any call between them is early for one side or late for the other.
pair.call.some.1: You have {duration} of shared working time: {fromRange} in {from}, which is {toRange} in {to}.
pair.call.some.2: The window is {duration} wide — {fromRange} in {from}, {toRange} in {to}.
pair.factsIntro.1: The underlying data, in case you need to put it in a calendar invitation or a configuration file.
pair.factsIntro.2: The zone identifiers and offsets behind everything above.
pair.faq.q.difference: What is the time difference between {from} and {to}?
pair.faq.a.difference.same: There is none. Both cities are in the {zone} time zone, so their clocks always read the same and change together.
pair.faq.a.difference.ahead: {to} is {gap} ahead of {from}. That figure is current — it changes by an hour when either city starts or ends daylight saving, and the exact dates are listed above.
pair.faq.a.difference.behind: {to} is {gap} behind {from}. That figure is current — it changes by an hour when either city starts or ends daylight saving, and the exact dates are listed above.
pair.faq.q.bestTime: When is the best time to call {to} from {from}?
pair.faq.a.bestTime.none: There is no time inside normal working hours in both cities, so someone has to take the call outside them. The nearest workable windows are listed above — pick one and alternate who gets the awkward slot.
pair.faq.a.bestTime.some: Between {fromRange} in {from}, which is {toRange} in {to}. That is the only stretch where both cities are inside a 09:00–18:00 day.
pair.faq.a.observesDst.yes: Yes. {city} runs on {standard} in winter and {daylight} in summer.
pair.faq.a.observesDst.yesNext: Yes. {city} runs on {standard} in winter and {daylight} in summer. The next change is on {date}, when clocks go {direction} by {minutes} minutes.
pair.faq.a.observesDst.no: No. {city} stays on {standard} all year, so its clocks never move.
pair.faq.q.midday: If it is midday in {from}, what time is it in {to}?
pair.faq.a.midday: It is {time} in {to}{dayClause}. That holds for the current offsets; {stability}.
pair.faq.stability.seasonal: it shifts by an hour around the daylight saving dates listed above
pair.faq.stability.fixed: it does not change through the year, because neither city moves its clocks
pair.faq.q.zones: Which time zones do {from} and {to} use?
pair.faq.a.zones: {from} uses {fromZone} (currently {fromAbbr}, {fromOffset}) and {to} uses {toZone} (currently {toAbbr}, {toOffset}). Those identifiers are the ones to use in code — abbreviations are ambiguous and offsets change.
city.summary.2: The current offset in {city} is {offset} ({abbr}), on the {zone} zone. {clause}
city.summary.clause.noDst: Its clocks never change, so that offset holds all year.
city.faq.a.zone: {city} uses the {zone} time zone, currently abbreviated {abbr} at {offset}. Use the IANA identifier rather than the abbreviation in code — abbreviations are ambiguous, and this one may mean something else somewhere else.
city.faq.a.dst.no: No. {city} keeps {standard} all year round, so its offset from UTC never changes.
city.faq.a.dst.yes: Yes. {city} moves between {standard} in winter and {daylight} in summer, changing {count} times in {year}.
city.faq.q.utcDiff: What is the difference between {city} and UTC?
city.faq.a.utcDiff.fixed: {offset} as of the last rebuild. That figure is constant, because the city does not change its clocks.
city.faq.a.utcDiff.varies: {offset} as of the last rebuild. It swings between {standard} and {daylight} across the year.
city.faq.q.sun: When does the sun rise and set in {city}?
city.faq.a.sun.polarDay: At this time of year the sun does not set in {city} — it stays above the horizon for the full 24 hours.
city.faq.a.sun.polarNight: At this time of year the sun does not rise in {city} — it stays below the horizon all day.
city.faq.a.sun.normal: On the day of the last rebuild, sunrise was {sunrise} and sunset {sunset} local time, giving {daylight} of daylight. These are computed from the city’s latitude and longitude, not fetched from anywhere.
